args.text:
RESTON, Va. – Heads up: from early October there'll be planes flying low over eastern California and a little sliver of western Nevada, taking a picture of the rocks underneath with some fancy airborne geophysics gear.

It's a joint effort between the U.S. Geological Survey's Earth Mapping Resources Initiative and the California Geological Survey (CGS). The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative is all about bringing the country's maps of geology and mineral resources up to date, and finding where the energy, the groundwater and the natural hazards are.

"Teaming up with the state surveys helps us get the national jobs done, like mapping the critical minerals the U.S. needs. The California Geological Survey is pitching in on the nation's work, and adding to what the state knows about things that really matter, like water, hazards and the resource economy," said Jamey Jones, science coordinator for the U.S. Geological Survey's Earth Mapping Resources Initiative.

"The Earth MRI datasets come out of a federal and state partnership working together to collect modern data in the parts of the state that matter most, put that data out there for anyone to use, and make a real difference to what we know about California's geology. This 2026 airborne geophysical survey is a big one, and it's over an area we've had our eye on for a few years now," said Jeremy Lancaster, California State Geologist and Director of the California Geological Survey.

The survey covers a chunk of eastern California on the western edge of the Great Basin, which has a whole mix of mineral deposits and mining districts with known resources in them, like the Pine Creek mine near Bishop, Calif., which has dug up more tungsten over the years than anywhere else in the U.S. There's still a fair bit left to find and dig up in the survey areas. The critical minerals and other goods they might turn up include antimony, arsenic, beryllium, bismuth, boron, copper, fluorine, gallium, germanium, graphite, indium, lead, lithium, mercury, molybdenum, potash, rubidium, silver, tellurium, tin, tungsten and zinc. Pretty much half the periodic table, really.

The new high-resolution surveys will give the basic geology data that future mineral exploration can build on, and they'll also give important data on what's under the ground for working out how much geothermal energy there might be, and the volcano and earthquake risks in the Long Valley caldera, along the front of the eastern Sierra Nevada range, and in Owens Valley.

The survey picks up magnetic and radiometric readings from helicopters flying set lines 660 feet (200 metres) apart, at a height of 330 feet (100 metres). The USGS has got NRG Exploration USA Inc. and Woolpert in to collect the magnetic and radiometric data from the air. Their AS350 choppers will have a long "stinger" sticking out from the main cabin or the skids, with the sensors that collect the data inside it. These science instruments are dead passive. They don't give off anything that's a risk to people, animals or plants. No photos or video will be taken, either, so no need to duck for cover in the backyard. The choppers will be flown by experienced pilots who've been specially trained and signed off for low-level flying. These pilots work with the FAA to make sure the flights are safe and done by the book under U.S. law. The surveys will only be flown in daylight.

The flights will go out of the Bishop and Lone Pine airports, and will fly over these counties: Fresno, Inyo and Mono in California, and Esmeralda and Mineral in Nevada.

Earth MRI covers airborne geophysical surveys like this one, geochemical reconnaissance surveys, topographic mapping with LiDAR technology, hyperspectral surveys and geologic mapping projects. The data they collect goes up free for anyone on the USGS ScienceBase website.
